questions.stem: Which side of the heart receives oxygenated blood from the lungs?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The right side receives deoxygenated blood from the body.
Oxygenated blood enters only the left atrium.
The blood returns to the heart via the pulmonary vein.

questions.stem: Why is the left ventricle's wall thicker than the right's?

options.explanation: Valves sit on both sides alike.

options.text: It drives blood at high pressure around the whole body
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Volume is similar; pressure is the difference.
Both ventricles beat together.
Coronary vessels run on the surface.
The septum never opens.

options.text: Separates the right and left sides of the heart
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Pumping is ventricular work.

questions.stem: Which vessels supply the heart muscle itself?

options.explanation: It delivers blood into the left atrium.
It returns blood to the right atrium.
The coronaries arise from the aorta's base but supply the muscle locally.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: What is the collective job of the heart's valves?

options.text: To prevent blood flowing backwards through the chambers
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Valves direct; momentum does the moving.

options.text: To filter oxygen into the muscle
options.explanation: No filtering or extraction happens at valves.
Valves lie between chambers and at the exits.

questions.stem: State the two circuits the double pump serves.
questions.modelAnswer: The right side serves the pulmonary circuit to the lungs and the left side serves the systemic circuit around the body.

questions.stem: Name the wall that divides the heart's sides.
questions.modelAnswer: The septum is the muscle wall dividing the heart's two sides.

questions.stem: Explain why the heart needs its own coronary supply despite being full of blood.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the blood inside the chambers passes too quickly and at the wrong pressures to nourish the muscle, so dedicated coronary arteries deliver oxygen and glucose directly.

questions.stem: A diagram shows the heart's left side on the viewer's right. Explain the labelling convention.
questions.modelAnswer: Diagrams label the heart as it sits in the chest, so the viewer's right shows the patient's left side and vice versa.

questions.stem: Through which vessel does deoxygenated blood enter the heart?

options.text: The pulmonary artery, into the right ventricle
options.explanation: The artery exits toward the lungs.

options.text: The vena cava, into the right atrium
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The pulmonary vein, into the left atrium
options.explanation: That is the oxygenated return.

options.text: The aorta, into the left ventricle
options.explanation: The aorta exits, not enters.

questions.stem: Which valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle?

options.explanation: Semilunar valves sit at the artery exits.
An atrioventricular valve guards each side.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The bicuspid sits on the left side.

questions.stem: Where does the blood go after leaving the right ventricle?

options.text: Into the aorta toward the body
options.explanation: The aorta is the left ventricle's exit.
Valves block that reverse step.
The left atrium receives blood only via the pulmonary vein.

options.text: Via the semilunar valve, out toward the lungs
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Why is blood pressure kept low on the right side?

options.text: To avoid damaging the delicate capillaries in the lungs
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because the lungs need no oxygen
options.explanation: The lungs' capillaries need steady, gentle flow.

options.text: To make the blood move faster
options.explanation: Lower pressure does not speed flow.
The septum is muscle, not capillary wall.

questions.stem: Through which valve and vessel does blood leave the left ventricle?

options.text: Through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium
options.explanation: That is an arrival, not a departure.

options.text: Through the semilunar valve into the aorta
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Through the bicuspid into the aorta
options.explanation: The bicuspid leads atrium-to-ventricle, not ventricle-to-artery.

options.text: Through the tricuspid into the pulmonary artery
options.explanation: Both names belong to the right side.

questions.stem: List the structures blood passes through on the right side, in order.
questions.modelAnswer: Vena cava, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, semilunar valve, pulmonary artery.

questions.stem: Name the valve and vessel pair on the left exit.
questions.modelAnswer: The semilunar valve opens into the aorta.

questions.stem: Explain why both atria and both ventricles contract together in the real heart, although the taught pathway follows one side at a time.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the sides work as one coordinated pump; the one-side-at-a-time account is only a teaching simplification, while in reality paired chambers contract together.

questions.stem: A drop of dye enters the vena cava. List its first four stops.
questions.modelAnswer: Right atrium, across the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, then out via the semilunar valve toward the lungs.
